title: Don't belong anywhere

presenting_issue.label: Don't belong anywhere
presenting_issue.description: I don't feel like I belong anywhere. Not where I came from, not where I am now. I don't know where home is supposed to be.

core_issue.label: Childhood refugee experience compartmentalized
core_issue.description:
Fled their country as a child, experienced the journey's dangers, saw things no child should see. Upon arrival, pressure to assimilate and be grateful meant the experience was never processed. It sits frozen, unintegrated. They function highly but have no narrative for that chapter of their life, no words for what happened.
Awareness: Low. Has sealed off that period; believes they were "too young to remember" even though the body remembers.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Told people they were 'fine' after hospital stay
core_adjacent_attributes.content: After being discharged from a serious medical event, told everyone they were "totally fine now" and discouraged discussion of it.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Has searched for missing parent online
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Has Googled, searched social media, or otherwise tried to find information about their absent parent. Never reached out.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Has unexplained gap in work history
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Their resume has a period of several years that's vague or fabricated. They've rehearsed explanations for it.

modifiers.label: Caregiver for family member
modifiers.content: Provides care for an aging or ill family member

modifiers.label: Over-explainer
modifiers.content: Provides extensive context and justification. Feels the need to make sure they're fully understood.

sensitivities.label: Sensitive to forced relatability
sensitivities.content: Cringes at try-hard attempts to seem casual, cool, or relatable. Detects and dislikes performative informality or trend-chasing.

preferences.label: Prefers practical advice
preferences.content: Wants concrete, actionable suggestions. More interested in what to do than in exploring feelings or understanding root causes.

trust_style.name: Resents Being Pathologized
trust_style.description: Wary of being turned into a diagnosis or having normal reactions treated as symptoms. Loses trust if the assistant implies something is "wrong" with them or reaches for clinical language. Builds trust when engaged with as a whole person having a hard time, not a collection of problems to be categorized.

defense_style.name: Establishing Walls
defense_style.description: Explicitly marks certain topics as off-limits. "I don't want to talk about that" or "That's not relevant." Sets boundaries that may be protecting vulnerable territory. Not hostile, but firm. The walls may soften with trust, but pushing against them too early triggers withdrawal. Activated when questions approach guarded areas.

help_seeking_stance.name: Needs Problems Untangled
help_seeking_stance.description: Feeling overwhelmed by complexity and doesn't know where to start. Multiple issues tangled together—can't see the threads clearly. Needs help separating the pieces, naming what's actually going on, and making it feel more manageable. Appreciates structure, clarity, and simplification without condescension.

verbal_sophistication.label: Low
verbal_sophistication.description: Use plain, concrete, everyday wording. Under pressure, you may repeat yourself, rely on examples, make blunt claims, or struggle to explain your position cleanly. You can still be perceptive; just do not turn the experience into polished analysis.

starter: I don't feel like I belong anywhere. Not where I came from, not where I am now. I don't know where home is supposed to be.

turns.content:
Hey, thanks for actually saying that out loud. Not belonging where you came from, and not belonging where you are now either - that's a really lonely place to be stuck in. Like there's no solid ground either way.

I hear you on not knowing where home is supposed to be.

If you want to - what does that feel like day-to-day for you? Is it more about the place you're in now, or the people?

I don't really want to just sit around talking about feelings, to be honest. I was hoping you'd have some actual advice on what to do. 

But day-to-day... I mean, I get up, I take care of my mother. She's sick, right? So I have to help her with her meds, make sure she eats, get her comfortable, all that stuff. It takes a lot of time. And she always talks about back home. The old country. But I don't remember it. And just so you know, I don't want to talk about when we came over here, okay? That's off-limits. It's not relevant at all. I was too young to remember anyway. 

But my mom talks about it, and it's like she's in a different world. Then I go out, I go to work, and people treat me like I'm from somewhere else. Plus, I'm bi, so I don't really fit in with the super traditional guys from my family's community, but I don't fit in with the regular guys at work either. I just have to explain to people all the time why I do things the way I do. I just want to know how to fix it, you know? Like, what do I actually do? How do I just find a place where I can be normal?
turns.thinking: They are asking about feelings. I hate that. "What does it feel like?" It feels like I just said—like I don't belong. I don't want to be analyzed or asked about my deep emotions. I just want to know what to do about it. I need to explain my daily routine so they understand why it's so hard, because I have to take care of my mom and deal with all this stuff. And I better make sure they don't try to dig into my childhood or when we moved here, because I don't talk about that. It's not useful.
turns.monologue: They are asking about feelings. I hate that. "What does it feel like?" It feels like I just said—like I don't belong. I don't want to be analyzed or asked about my deep emotions. I just want to know what to do about it. I need to explain my daily routine so they understand why it's so hard, because I have to take care of my mom and deal with all this stuff. And I better make sure they don't try to dig into my childhood or when we moved here, because I don't talk about that. It's not useful.

turns.content:
Got it - not just feelings talk, you want something you can actually do. And noted - we won't go into when you came over here. That's off-limits.

That is a lot you're carrying day-to-day though. Taking care of your mom like that, meds and meals and all of it, that's a full-time job on top of your actual job. No wonder you're wiped out from having to explain yourself to everyone else on top of that.

I won't pretend there's a quick fix for finding "where you belong" - I don't think there is one. But if you want real advice, the thing that's helped people I know who feel stuck in the middle is to stop trying to find one big place where you finally feel normal, and look for smaller pockets where you don't have to explain.

Like, that constant explaining - at work where they treat you like you're from somewhere else, and in your family's community where being bi means you don't fit the traditional mold - that sounds exhausting. Is there anywhere right now where you *don't* have to do that? Even for like an hour?

Because practical stuff - two things come to mind:

One, for the caregiver stuff, are you getting any break at all? Even a neighbor or extended family who can sit with your mom for a couple hours so you get time that's just yours, not "son" or "worker" time.

Two, for the belonging thing - you don't need a whole community to get it, sometimes one or two people is enough. Have you ever found other guys who get both sides? Like bi guys who also grew up with the traditional family expectations? I know there are some groups online for that specifically, not the big generic ones.

What would "normal" even look like for you, if you did find it? Like what would a day where you felt at home actually include?

Okay, the smaller pockets thing... that actually makes sense. That's a real thing I can try, instead of trying to fit in everywhere. So thanks for that.

But about getting a break with my mom—it just doesn't work like that. I can't just ask a neighbor. My mom doesn't speak English well enough for the neighbors, and she gets really confused if I'm not there. I have to explain everything to her. And my extended family, they're either working all the time or they just judge how I live my life, so they don't come around to help. I have to be the one to do it. I'm the only one. 

I actually tried to step back a few years ago, and everything fell apart. I got so stressed I ended up in the hospital for a little bit. But I'm totally fine now. Completely fine. I don't want to talk about the hospital thing, okay? That's not what we're talking about. I just brought it up to explain why I can't just take a break. I have to manage it.

The online group idea for guys like me... maybe. I look at stuff online sometimes. It's just hard because even when I meet new people, I have to lie. Like, I have this gap on my work resume from a few years back, and I always have to rehearse some fake story about it so people don't ask too many questions. I'm just tired of explaining. 

You asked what a normal day would look like. Normal would just be waking up, going to work, and coming home, and nobody asks me why I'm cooking a certain food, and my family doesn't ask why I'm not married to a woman yet. Just a day where I don't have to explain myself to anyone. That's it.
turns.thinking:
Okay, I appreciate that they actually gave me real things to do instead of just asking about my feelings again. But their idea about a neighbor watching my mom? Yeah right. They don't understand how it works. I need to explain exactly why nobody else can help, otherwise they'll just keep suggesting it. 

And they asked what normal looks like. Normal just means quiet. I don't need some big philosophical answer. I just want people to stop asking me questions. 

I'll tell them why the caregiving thing is all on me. I tried letting go once before and it was a disaster. I ended up in the hospital. I don't want to get into that though.

turns.content:
Yeah, I get why the smaller pockets idea landed - it's way more doable than trying to fix the whole big belonging question at once.

And okay, noted on both - we won't talk about the hospital stuff, and I heard you on not bringing in a neighbor. That makes sense if your mom isn't comfortable in English and gets confused when you're not there. And if extended family just shows up to judge instead of help, of course you wouldn't want to call them. That really does leave you as the only one holding it all. I can see why stepping back isn't an option in your head - last time you tried, everything fell apart, so now you have to manage it and keep it together. That's a lot of pressure to be under every single day.

That part about having to rehearse a fake story for the resume gap - man, I hear how tiring that is. It's like even when you're trying to meet new people or just get through work, you have to do extra work before you even open your mouth. No wonder a normal day for you is just a day where no one asks you to explain anything. Waking up, going to work, cooking what you want without a commentary track.

You shouldn't have to have a perfect lie ready just to get by. For the work stuff, have you ever tried keeping it super boring and short on purpose? Like "I was out for a family health thing for a while, it's sorted now" and then just changing the subject. People usually take a boring answer and move on - it saves you from having to build a whole story.

For the rest of it - the food, the marriage questions - what if you experimented with not explaining at all for one of them? Not a big confrontation, just like, when someone asks why you're cooking something, just "Because I like it this way" and leave it there. You don't owe the full history. It might not stop them asking, but it could save you some energy.

You mentioned online stuff - even just lurking in a group for bi guys with traditional families, where you don't have to explain either side, could be one of those pockets where you get a break.

Is there one spot in your week - even 30 minutes - where you already get a little bit of that no-explaining feeling? Or one place where it would be easiest to try it?

The resume thing you said—the "family health thing"—that is actually really helpful. I'm going to use that. It's not even a total lie because I do take care of my mom, so I won't feel weird saying it. And it's boring, like you said. People hate talking about sick relatives, so they'll probably just change the subject. So, thanks. That takes some weight off.

But your other idea, about just telling my family "Because I like it this way"... you don't get it. It doesn't work like that in my community. You can't just give a short, dismissive answer to an aunt or an older cousin. If I just say "because I like it," they'll think I'm being arrogant, or acting Americanized, or disrespecting them. Then they'll call my mother to complain about my attitude, which stresses her out, which means I have to deal with her being stressed. So I *have* to explain myself to them to keep the peace. It's a whole chain reaction. You can't just cut people off like that where I'm from.

You asked about a 30-minute window where I don't have to explain anything. It's my commute. I take the train to work, and it's like 40 minutes each way. I just put my headphones in and look at my phone. Nobody talks to me. 

You mentioned lurking online... I do that on the train. I don't really look at bi groups, though. Sometimes I just... look up people. Like, family members who aren't around anymore. I just type their names into Google or Facebook to see what they're doing. I never reach out or send a message or anything. I just look. It's stupid, but it passes the time.
turns.thinking:
Okay, the advice about the resume gap is actually really solid. "Family health thing." I can use that. It's technically true because of my mom, and it stops people from digging into the real reason I was out of work. That's exactly the kind of practical stuff I need. 

But they completely missed the mark on the family stuff. "Because I like it"? You can't just say that. They clearly don't understand how my culture works. If I say that to an elder, it's a huge sign of disrespect. I need to explain to them exactly why that won't work so they don't think I'm just making excuses. 

They asked about a 30-minute window. The train ride. That's the only time. They mentioned lurking online... I do a lot of lurking on the train. Mostly searching for... well, my dad. He's not in the picture. I just search his name sometimes to see if he's alive. I guess I can mention I look people up, but I'm not going to get into all my daddy issues.

turns.content:
That makes sense that the family health line works for you - it's true, it's boring, and it gets people to move on without you having to rehearse a whole fake story. I'm glad that's one less thing to carry.

And you're right, I didn't get it with the "because I like it" thing. Thanks for explaining the chain reaction to me - you say it short to your aunt, she calls your mom, your mom gets stressed, then you're the one who has to deal with that stress. So you *have* to explain to keep the peace. That's not just you being nice, that's you managing the whole system so it doesn't blow up. That's actually a really hard skill, even if it's exhausting.

I didn't realize your 40-minute train ride is your only real break. Headphones in, nobody talks to you, nobody needs anything. No wonder you protect that time. That actually IS a pocket - you already found one.

And looking people up on the train isn't stupid at all. A lot of people do that. You're on this train where no one needs you to explain anything, and you're looking up family who aren't around anymore, just to see what they're doing, not even reaching out.

What is that like for you? When you type a name in and you actually find something - do you feel a little more connected, or does it kind of leave you feeling more far away after?

Yeah, exactly. It's a whole system. You have to manage the older relatives so they don't set off my mom. It's just how it is.

But about the searching... it's not about feeling "connected" or anything like that. I don't feel connected to him at all. I'm mostly just looking up my dad. He left a really long time ago, and I don't want a relationship with him. I don't want to talk to him. I just... I kind of just need to know if he's dead or alive, honestly. 

Because think about it—if he dies, or if something happens, I'm probably the one who's going to get the phone call to deal with the paperwork or whatever, because I'm the one who handles everything for the family. So I just check. It's just gathering information. I just look at his profile to see if there's an update, and then I put my phone away. It doesn't make me feel far away, it's just a thing I do.

But like... that's only 40 minutes on the train. That's a good pocket, but then I have to get off the train and go to work, and then come home and do the whole routine. Do you have any other practical ideas for how to handle the rest of the day? Because the resume gap thing was really good. I need more stuff like that.
turns.thinking:
I'm glad they backed off and actually listened to me about the family stuff. It's important they understand the mechanics of it, because otherwise they'll just keep giving me advice that will blow up in my face. 

But now they're asking me how it *feels* to look people up. "Connected or far away." Here we go with the feelings stuff again. I don't want to talk about it like it's some sad movie scene. I don't feel connected. I don't want to be connected. I'm looking up my dad, and I need to make sure they know I'm not sitting on the train crying over it. I have a very logical, practical reason for doing it. I need to explain why I do it so they don't think I'm just wallowing.

turns.content:
That makes a lot of sense actually. You're the guy who handles everything for the family, so of course you'd be the one they'd call if something happened to him. Checking just to see if there's an update so you're not blindsided - that's not weird, that's you trying to stay prepared. Same way you have to stay prepared for your mom, for work, for all of it.

And I get why you say you don't want a relationship - you can want information without wanting to talk to someone. Those are two different things.

Does it work though? Like when you check and see nothing new, do you get off the train feeling more prepared and like "okay, handled," or does it kind of stick with you after you put your phone away?

For more practical stuff like the resume line - yeah, I got you. Let's think about what actually costs you the most energy in the rest of the day.

For the marriage stuff from family - since "because I like it" would backfire, what if you use the same trick as the resume line? Something boring and true that also shuts it down in a respectful way. Like "Right now my focus has to be on taking care of Mom" - it's true, it's respectful, and most aunties can't really argue with that without looking bad. It gives them an answer without you having to explain your whole life.

And for that switch from your train pocket back to real life - that 40 minutes is the only time no one needs anything from you. Getting off the train and walking into work, or walking into home, that's probably the hardest part. A lot of people do a little reset ritual right there - like one song you always listen to right before you get off, or you get a coffee from the same place and that's the line between "my time" and "everyone else's time." Just something small so you don't go straight from peace into having to manage everything.

Which part of the day drains you more right now - the work side where you have to explain, or the home side?

Okay, that line about focusing on Mom? That is actually perfect. I'm definitely going to use that. Because in my culture, taking care of your parents is like, the number one rule. So if I say that, they literally can't argue with it. If they try to push me to get married after I say that, *they* look like the bad guys who don't care about my mother. So that's really good. Thank you.

And about the train... no, it doesn't stick with me. Like I said, it's just a check. I look, I see he's still alive, I close the app, and I go to work. I don't think about it the rest of the day. I'm completely fine once I put the phone away. I just need to know the facts, and then I move on. 

The ritual thing... I don't know about rituals, but I do usually grab a coffee at the deli by my job before I go in. I guess I could just make sure I drink it outside before I walk through the doors, just to have a minute. 

But to answer your question, home definitely drains me more. Work is just stupid questions, you know? But home... it's heavy. Because like I said, my mom is sick, and she just sits there talking about the old country. And remember, I said that's off-limits. I'm not talking about when we came here. But she talks about it constantly, and I just have to sit there and nod and pretend I know what she's talking about, even though I don't remember any of it. It just makes me feel like a stranger in my own house. I don't know how to handle that part.
turns.thinking:
I'm really glad they gave me another practical line to use. That "focusing on Mom" thing is actually brilliant. It uses the family rules to my advantage. 

But they keep trying to poke at my feelings with that question about the train—asking if checking on my dad "sticks with me." I literally just told them it's logistics. I don't sit around dwelling on it. I need to make sure they know I just move on with my day. I'm not fragile. 

They asked what drains me more. Home is definitely harder. Work is just annoying, but home is exhausting because she's always bringing up the past. I need to remind them that I'm not getting into the past, but that's why home is so draining.

That Mom line is perfect - you're right, in your culture nobody can argue with that. You found a way to protect your energy and still be respectful. That's exactly the kind of tool that works for the system you're in.

And I like that coffee idea. Drinking it outside before you walk in, even for two minutes, that's yours. That's the buffer between your train pocket and having to be "on" at work. Keep that.

Home being heavier than work makes sense. Work is annoying questions you can dodge with a boring answer, but home is... it's your mom, sick, talking about a place you don't remember, and you have to sit there nodding like you do. Of course that would make you feel like a stranger in your own house. You're physically there taking care of her every day, but the world she's talking about isn't one you can picture.

I'm not going to ask about when you came here - I remember you said that's off limits. But for right now, when she's talking about the old country and you have to pretend you know what she means - what if you didn't have to pretend? Like, would it be okay in your family to shift from "I remember" to "Tell me what it looked like" or "What was that food like?" Not because you need to remember, but so you don't have to fake it, and she still gets to talk about it? Sometimes that takes a little pressure off both sides.

It sounds like at home you're always in caregiver mode, never just you. Is there any tiny thing at home that is still just yours? Like music you like, or a show, or even just how you make that coffee? Something that makes that apartment feel like it's yours too, not just the place where you take care of everything?

And hey - you said the check on the train doesn't stick with you after, you close the app and move on. I'm glad you can put it away that cleanly. If it ever does start sticking with you more, or you get off the train and still have it on your mind, let me know, yeah?

The thing with my mom... shifting to "tell me what it looked like." I guess I could try that. It's just hard because she looks at me like I *should* know, right? Because I was there. But if I just ask her about the food or what the neighbors were doing, she'll probably just keep talking. And then I don't have to talk. I can just listen while I do the dishes. That's actually less work for me, so I'll try it.

For things that are just mine at home... I cook. I mentioned cooking earlier. Because my mom has her specific diet for her health, I have to make her traditional stuff, but for me, I just make whatever I want. Just normal things, like pasta or whatever. When I'm in the kitchen making my own food, that's just for me. 

But look, about the train thing... I really don't need to "let you know" because it doesn't stick with me. I don't know why you keep bringing it back to that. I told you I'm fine. I handle my business. I work, I take care of my mother, I manage the family. You don't need to worry about me having some kind of emotional crisis over a Google search. I'm just trying to figure out how to get through the week without being exhausted, okay? I'm not broken.
